summary.text: Quadratic reciprocity shows that for such a prime, 5 is a quadratic residue, so one may choose \(4\le m<p\) with \(m^2\equiv5\pmod p\). A continuant invariant identifies the raw numerator at index \(m-1\) as \(m^2-5=p t\); its recurrence shows that the cofactor \(t\) divides the denominator continuant while \(p\) does not (otherwise divisibility propagates to the terminal value \(-1\)), so reduction leaves numerator—and hence the desired denominator—equal to \(p\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
R_k(n)=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}(n)}
\]
for \(2\le k<n-1\), with terminal value
\[
R_{n-1}(n)=(n-1)-\frac n{-4}=(n-1)+\frac n4.
\]
Thus the continued fraction defining the sequence is \(1/R_2(n)\). If \(R_2(n)=N/D\) in lowest terms, then \(1/R_2(n)=D/N\), so \(a(n)=|N|\).

We will prove that every prime \(p\equiv 1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\) occurs by finding an integer \(m\), with \(4\le m<p\), such that
\[
m^2\equiv 5\pmod p,
\]
and then showing that \(a(m-1)=p\).

## 1. Integer continuants

For an integer \(m\ge4\), define integers \(E_m(k)\) backwards by
\[
E_m(m)=-1,\qquad E_m(m-1)=4,
\]
and, for \(k\le m-2\),
\[
E_m(k)=kE_m(k+1)-(k+1)E_m(k+2). \tag{1}
\]
These integers encode the numerator and denominator of the tails of the continued fraction.

The main identity governing them is
\[
(k-1)E_m(k)-k(k-2)E_m(k+1)=m^2-5 \tag{2}
\]
for every \(2\le k\le m-1\).

We prove (2) by descending induction on \(k\). At \(k=m-1\), the left side is
\[
(m-2)E_m(m-1)-(m-1)(m-3)E_m(m)
=4(m-2)+(m-1)(m-3)=m^2-5.
\]
Now suppose the identity is known at \(k+1\). Using (1), its left side at \(k\) becomes
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(k-1)\bigl(kE_m(k+1)-(k+1)E_m(k+2)\bigr)
   -k(k-2)E_m(k+1)\\
&=kE_m(k+1)-(k+1)(k-1)E_m(k+2),
\end{aligned}
\]
which is exactly the left side of (2) with \(k+1\) in place of \(k\). This proves the invariant.

In particular, taking \(k=2\) in (2) gives
\[
E_m(2)=m^2-5. \tag{3}
\]

We will also need positivity. For \(m\ge4\),
\[
E_m(k)>0\qquad(2\le k\le m-1). \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, \(E_m(m-1)=4>0\). Descending from \(k+1\) to \(k\), identity (2) can be rearranged as
\[
(k-1)E_m(k)=m^2-5+k(k-2)E_m(k+1).
\]
Here \(m^2-5>0\), the second term on the right is nonnegative, and \(k-1>0\). Hence \(E_m(k)>0\), proving (4).

We next identify the continued fraction tails. For \(2\le k\le m-2\),
\[
R_k(m-1)=\frac{E_m(k)}{E_m(k+1)}. \tag{5}
\]
At the terminal index \(k=m-2\),
\[
R_{m-2}(m-1)=(m-2)+\frac{m-1}{4}
=\frac{4(m-2)+(m-1)}4.
\]
On the other hand, (1) and the boundary values give
\[
E_m(m-2)=4(m-2)-(m-1)(-1)=4(m-2)+(m-1),
\]
while \(E_m(m-1)=4\), so (5) holds at the terminal index. If it holds at \(k+1\), then, using the recurrence for the continued fraction and the fact that the positive integers \(E_m(k+1),E_m(k+2)\) are nonzero,
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_k(m-1)
&=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}(m-1)}\\
&=k-(k+1)\frac{E_m(k+2)}{E_m(k+1)}\\
&=\frac{kE_m(k+1)-(k+1)E_m(k+2)}{E_m(k+1)}\\
&=\frac{E_m(k)}{E_m(k+1)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus (5) follows by descending induction. In particular, by (3),
\[
R_2(m-1)=\frac{m^2-5}{E_m(3)}. \tag{6}
\]
Both numerator and denominator in (6) are positive when \(m\ge4\).

## 2. Divisibility properties of the denominator continuant

We need two complementary facts about \(E_m(3)\).

### Proper small divisors are absorbed by the denominator

Suppose
\[
3\le d<m,\qquad d\mid m^2-5.
\]
Then
\[
d\mid E_m(3). \tag{7}
\]

Apply the invariant (2) at \(k=d\):
\[
(d-1)E_m(d)-d(d-2)E_m(d+1)=m^2-5.
\]
The right side is divisible by \(d\), as is the second term on the left. Consequently
\[
d\mid (d-1)E_m(d).
\]
Since consecutive integers are coprime, \(\gcd(d,d-1)=1\), so
\[
d\mid E_m(d). \tag{8}
\]
We now propagate this divisibility downwards. Suppose \(3\le k<d\), and the needed divisibility has already been established at higher indices. From (1),
\[
E_m(k)=kE_m(k+1)-(k+1)E_m(k+2).
\]
If \(k+1<d\), both \(E_m(k+1)\) and \(E_m(k+2)\) are divisible by \(d\), so the right side is divisible by \(d\). If \(k+1=d\), the first term is divisible by \(d\) by (8), and the coefficient \(k+1=d\) makes the second term divisible by \(d\) as well. Descending to \(k=3\) proves (7).

### A large prime divisor is not absorbed

Suppose \(p\) is prime, \(3\le m<p\), and
\[
p\mid m^2-5.
\]
Then
\[
p\nmid E_m(3). \tag{9}
\]

Assume for contradiction that \(p\mid E_m(3)\). We show inductively that
\[
p\mid E_m(k)\qquad(3\le k\le m).
\]
The assertion starts at \(k=3\). Suppose \(4\le k\le m\) and \(p\mid E_m(k-1)\). Apply (2) at \(k-1\):
\[
(k-2)E_m(k-1)-(k-1)(k-3)E_m(k)=m^2-5.
\]
The right side and the first term on the left are divisible by \(p\), so
\[
p\mid (k-1)(k-3)E_m(k).
\]
Both positive integers \(k-1\) and \(k-3\) are strictly less than \(p\), because \(k\le m<p\). Since \(p\) is prime, neither is divisible by \(p\), and each is therefore coprime to \(p\). Cancelling them yields \(p\mid E_m(k)\). The induction reaches \(k=m\), but \(E_m(m)=-1\), which no prime divides. This contradiction proves (9).

## 3. A suitable root produces exactly the prime \(p\)

We now prove the central implication. Let \(p\) be prime and suppose that
\[
4\le m<p,\qquad m^2\equiv5\pmod p. \tag{10}
\]
Then
\[
a(m-1)=p. \tag{11}
\]

Because \(m\ge4\), the integer \(m^2-5\) is positive. Congruence (10) says that \(p\mid m^2-5\), so write
\[
m^2-5=pt \tag{12}
\]
with \(t\) a positive integer.

We first note that
\[
t<m. \tag{13}
\]
Indeed, since \(m<p\) and \(m>0\), we have \(m^2<mp\). Hence
\[
pt=m^2-5<m^2<mp,
\]
and cancellation of the positive factor \(p\) gives (13).

We claim that
\[
t\mid E_m(3). \tag{14}
\]
If \(t\ge3\), this follows immediately from (13), (12), and the small-divisor result (7). It remains to consider \(t<3\). Since \(t>0\), it is either \(1\) or \(2\). The value \(1\) plainly divides \(E_m(3)\). We show that \(t=2\) is impossible.

If \(t=2\), then
\[
m^2-5=2p. \tag{15}
\]
First, \(p\ne2\): if \(p=2\), (15) gives \(m^2=9\), impossible for \(m\ge4\). Thus \(p\) is odd. If \(m\) is even, then \(m^2-5\) is odd, whereas \(2p\) is even, contradicting (15). If \(m\) is odd, then \(m^2\equiv1\pmod4\), so \(m^2-5\equiv0\pmod4\); but for odd \(p\), \(2p\equiv2\pmod4\), again contradicting (15). Therefore \(t\ne2\), and (14) holds in every case.

On the other hand, the large-prime result (9), applied using \(m<p\), gives
\[
p\nmid E_m(3). \tag{16}
\]
Since \(E_m(3)>0\), write \(E_m(3)=tu\), which is possible by (14), with \(u>0\). Equation (16) implies \(p\nmid u\), and because \(p\) is prime this means \(\gcd(p,u)=1\). Substituting (12) into (6), we obtain
\[
R_2(m-1)=\frac{pt}{tu}=\frac pu.
\]
The last fraction is in lowest terms because \(\gcd(p,u)=1\). Its numerator is the positive integer \(p\). As observed at the outset, the denominator of the reciprocal continued fraction \(1/R_2(m-1)\) is the absolute value of this reduced numerator. Hence
\[
a(m-1)=p,
\]
which proves (11).

## 4. Producing the required root of 5

It remains to show that every prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\) admits an \(m\) satisfying (10).

First, such a prime is greater than \(9\). Indeed, a positive integer congruent to \(1\pmod {10}\) that is at most \(9\) can only be \(1\), and one congruent to \(9\pmod {10}\) that is at most \(9\) can only be \(9\); neither is prime. In particular, \(p\) is an odd prime distinct from \(5\).

Reduction modulo \(5\) gives
\[
p\equiv1\quad\hbox{or}\quad4\pmod5. \tag{17}
\]
Both residues are nonzero squares modulo \(5\): \(1\equiv1^2\pmod5\) and \(4\equiv2^2\pmod5\). Thus the Legendre symbol satisfies
\[
\left(\frac p5\right)=1.
\]
By quadratic reciprocity, for distinct odd primes \(p\) and \(5\),
\[
\left(\frac5p\right)\left(\frac p5\right)
=(-1)^{((5-1)/2)((p-1)/2)}.
\]
Since \((5-1)/2=2\) is even, the sign on the right is \(1\). Therefore
\[
\left(\frac5p\right)=\left(\frac p5\right)=1.
\]
Consequently, \(5\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\). There is thus a residue class \(x\pmod p\) satisfying
\[
x^2\equiv5\pmod p.
\]
Let \(m\) be its standard representative with
\[
0\le m<p.
\]
We claim that \(m\ge4\). Since \(p>9\), each of \(0,1,4,5,9\) is already its own least nonnegative residue modulo \(p\). If \(m=0,1,2,3\), then \(m^2\) is respectively \(0,1,4,9\), none of which is congruent to \(5\pmod p\): because both numbers being compared lie between \(0\) and \(p-1\), such a congruence would force literal equality. Hence \(m\notin\{0,1,2,3\}\), so
\[
4\le m<p,
\]
and by construction \(m^2\equiv5\pmod p\).

Applying the result of Section 3 gives
\[
a(m-1)=p.
\]
Thus, with \(n=m-1\), every prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\) occurs in A363347, as required.
